subtype: Approach: arguing on and on with no decision [Pitfall]
passage: In the Class 7 room of their Delhi school, Saurabh, Suraj and two others had one period to start their poster on saving water. Saurabh wanted the title 'Every Drop Counts'. Suraj wanted 'Save Water, Save Life'. That took fifteen minutes. Then colours: blue and white, or green and blue? Someone suggested yellow and was shouted down. The chart paper lay blank in the middle of the desk, one corner curling. When the bell rang, all they had was a pencil line where a title might go. Ms Kaur stopped at their desk. 'Friday is the deadline,' she said, looking at the empty sheet. Suraj stared at his shoes.

qa.q: What title did Saurabh want?
qa.a: 'Every Drop Counts'.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when Ms Kaur looked at the empty sheet?
qa.a: Staring at his shoes suggests he felt embarrassed and a bit worried about Friday.

qa.q: What would you change first in how the group worked?
qa.a: Set a short time limit for choosing the title and colours, or vote, so arguing doesn't eat the whole period.

qa.q: How does Ms Kaur see the group's period?
qa.a: Ms Kaur sees a blank sheet after a whole period and reminds them about Friday, so she's likely concerned they're falling behind.

grounding: Shows a group arguing all period over a title and colours, making nothing before the bell, and the teacher reminding them the deadline is Friday.

subtype: Approach: arguing on and on with no decision [Pitfall]
passage:
"The title should be 'Our Green Planet'."
"Too boring. 'Earth Needs You!'"
"With an exclamation mark? Irfan, that sounds like an advert."
"And yours sounds like a textbook."
"Fine, colours then. Green."
"Green is obvious. Purple."
"Purple for the earth, Irfan?"
"It's creative!"
"It's wrong!"
The other two in the group had started drawing cartoons in the margins of their notebooks.
BRRRING.
"Wait, the period's over?"
Ma'am came to their table and looked at the chart paper. It was completely white. "Remember, Friday is the deadline."
Jaya and Irfan looked at each other. Neither of them said anything now.

qa.q: What colour did Irfan suggest?
qa.a: Purple.

qa.q: How did Jaya and Irfan feel when they saw the chart was still white?
qa.a: They fell silent and looked at each other, so they seemed embarrassed and worried about the Friday deadline.

qa.q: What could the group try next period?
qa.a: Give themselves five minutes to agree and then vote, or let the other two decide; arguing about every choice left nothing made.

qa.q: What was the period like for the other two in the group?
qa.a: They gave up and drew cartoons in their notebooks, so they seemed bored and shut out of the argument.

grounding: Illustrates a group arguing over title and colours for a whole period, finishing with a blank chart and a reminder that the deadline is Friday.

subtype: Approach: setting a time limit for deciding [Action]
passage: Teacher's note, group work, Tuesday. Group 3 had been circling for ten minutes: volcanoes or the moon? Then Jaya stood up and said, 'Five minutes. If we can't decide by then, we toss a coin.' She put her watch on the desk. Charu argued for the moon for two minutes, Jaya for volcanoes for two, and the others said they didn't mind. At five minutes there was still no decision, so Jaya tossed a coin. Moon. Jaya shrugged, 'Okay, moon,' and they started sketching craters right away. It was the first group with a title today. I'll share the five-minute idea with the other groups.

qa.q: Which two topics was Group 3 circling between?
qa.a: Volcanoes or the moon.

qa.q: How did Jaya seem to feel when the coin chose the moon?
qa.a: She shrugged and said 'Okay, moon', so she seemed at ease, content that a decision was made even though her choice lost.

qa.q: Why did the five-minute limit work?
qa.a: It stopped the endless talk; with a coin as backup, the group had to settle it and could start sketching right away.

qa.q: How might Charu see the coin toss?
qa.a: Charu's moon won, so Charu may feel pleased, and the toss made the result feel fair rather than a win in an argument.

grounding: Shows a girl giving her group five minutes to choose a topic, with a coin toss as backup, which ends the endless talk and gets them started.

subtype: Approach: setting a time limit for deciding [Action]
passage:
Thursday
Science project meeting at lunch. Yogesh wanted solar energy, I wanted plants, and the other two kept switching sides. After fifteen minutes I said, 'Okay, five minutes on the clock. If we don't agree, coin toss. Heads solar, tails plants.' Yogesh said, 'Vinita, you're so bossy,' but he agreed. He made his case again. I made mine. At four minutes we were still stuck. The coin came up heads. Solar. I felt a little flat, I'll be honest, but by the end of lunch we'd already divided the jobs, and I'm doing the diagram of the panel. Better than another week of arguing.

qa.q: What did heads stand for?
qa.a: Heads stood for solar.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when the coin came up heads?
qa.a: Vinita felt a little flat and disappointed, but relieved the arguing was over and the group could start.

qa.q: What did the group do right after the toss, and why did it help?
qa.a: They divided the jobs straight away, so the time limit and coin turned into real progress, not just an ended argument.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel about the result?
qa.a: Yogesh's solar idea won, so he likely felt pleased, even though he had called the timer bossy.

grounding: Illustrates a girl setting a five-minute limit with a coin toss as backup, which stops the endless talk and gets the group working.

subtype: Approach: one member doing everything alone [Pitfall]
passage:
Tuesday, 1:10 am
I just finished the whole model of the solar-powered house. Alone. Tanvir and the others kept saying 'tomorrow, tomorrow', and I was so fed up I decided to do it myself. Started at eight. Cut the cardboard, glued the roof, painted the panels. Mummy came in at eleven and said, 'Abhinav beta, sleep,' but I kept going. It looks really good.
Tuesday evening
I fell asleep in maths. Tanvir looked hurt when he saw the model and said, 'You didn't even call us.' The others didn't talk to me at lunch. Ma'am asked who made what. I said me. She frowned and said group work means the group.

qa.q: When did Abhinav finish the model?
qa.a: Abhinav finished it at 1:10 am, alone.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel before deciding to do it alone?
qa.a: Abhinav was fed up and annoyed with the group's 'tomorrow, tomorrow'.

qa.q: What could Abhinav have done instead of working through the night?
qa.a: Tell the group he was worried about time and set a deadline, or ask the teacher for help; doing it alone left him exhausted and the others shut out.

qa.q: How does Tanvir see the finished model?
qa.a: Tanvir looks hurt and says 'You didn't even call us', so he feels left out of his own group's project.

grounding: Shows a boy, annoyed by delays, finishing the group project alone at night, ending up exhausted while the others feel left out and the teacher notices.

subtype: Approach: one member doing everything alone [Pitfall]
passage: The group project on the village pond was due Monday, and Wasim was tired of waiting. Sachin kept going off to the fields; the others hadn't even collected leaves. On Saturday night, by the light of the kerosene lamp, Wasim did everything himself: the map of the pond, the list of birds, the drawing of the lotus, the neat heading. He went to bed after the roosters had started. On Monday the chart was the best in the class. But Wasim was yawning in the prayer line, and Sachin, looking at the chart, said, 'So we're not needed.' Masterji asked the group to explain the birds list. Only Wasim could. Masterji looked at the others for a long moment.

qa.q: What was the group project about?
qa.a: The village pond.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt yawning in the prayer line?
qa.a: He was exhausted from working till the roosters started, and probably still resentful that the others hadn't helped.

qa.q: What would have been a better way for Wasim to handle the delays?
qa.a: Split the jobs and give each person a day to finish, or ask Masterji for help; doing everything alone cost him sleep and cut out the group.

qa.q: How does Sachin feel when he sees the chart?
qa.a: Sachin says 'So we're not needed', which suggests he felt left out and a little hurt.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who, fed up with delays, does the whole group project alone at night, leaving him exhausted and the others left out.

subtype: Approach: asking the teacher to settle a stuck point [Revision]
passage: Teacher's note, Wednesday. Rekha's group came to my desk at break today. Rekha spoke for them: 'Ma'am, we've been arguing for two days about whether to do the project on birds or on trees, and we're stuck. Can you help?' I was glad they came. I asked each of them to tell me their idea in one minute, one at a time, no interrupting. Sudha went first, for trees, then the others. It became clear that three of the four preferred trees but had been too loud to hear each other. They chose trees, with a bird corner for Rekha. I also reminded them: one voice at a time at their next meeting.

qa.q: What two topics was the group arguing about?
qa.a: Birds or trees.

qa.q: How did Rekha seem to feel when she spoke for the group?
qa.a: Rekha seemed frustrated at being stuck but hopeful, asking plainly for help.

qa.q: Why did going to the teacher help after two days?
qa.a: The teacher gave each person a turn to speak, which showed three of the four preferred trees, something they couldn't hear while all talking at once.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see the group coming to the desk?
qa.a: The note-writer was glad they came, seeing it as a sensible step once they were stuck.

grounding: Shows a group that, after two days without agreement, notices it is stuck and asks the teacher, who helps them choose and reminds them to take turns.

subtype: Approach: asking the teacher to settle a stuck point [Revision]
passage:
Friday
Our group has been fighting about the history project since Wednesday. Raghav wants a play about the old spice traders, I want a timeline, and the other two just want it to be over. Today at lunch I noticed we were saying exactly the same things as on Wednesday, only louder. We're not getting anywhere. So I said, 'Let's ask Mrs Pinto.' We went to the staff room together. She said, 'Reena, what's the problem?' and listened to all of us. Then she asked, 'Can a timeline be acted out?' Suddenly it was obvious: a timeline play, each scene on a different date. Then she added, 'And next time, one person talks at a time.' Raghav actually laughed.

qa.q: What did Raghav want to do?
qa.a: A play about the old spice traders.

qa.q: What did Reena notice at lunch, and how did it feel?
qa.a: Reena felt frustrated, noticing they were repeating Wednesday's arguments, only louder, and saw they were stuck.

qa.q: Why was asking Mrs Pinto a good step?
qa.a: After days of going round in circles, one question from outside showed them a plan that combined both ideas.

qa.q: How did Raghav seem to feel about the new plan?
qa.a: Raghav laughed at the reminder, so he seemed relieved and happy with a play that kept his idea.

grounding: Illustrates a group noticing after days of arguing that they are stuck, and asking the teacher, who helps them pick a plan and reminds them to take turns.

subtype: Approach: checking in halfway and reassigning slow tasks [Revision]
passage:
Wednesday
Halfway to the deadline, so I made our group show what we'd done so far. Drawings, done. Nisha's map, done. Gurpreet's part, the four paragraphs, not started. He'd had fever all last week and looked worried saying it. Instead of getting cross, we split his paragraphs: Nisha takes two, I take two. Gurpreet will stick everything on the chart and write the headings, which is easier. He looked so relieved and said, 'Thanks, Kunal.'
Friday
Finished! On time, even a day early. Gurpreet's headings are the neatest part of the whole chart.

qa.q: Why hadn't Gurpreet started his paragraphs?
qa.a: He'd had fever all last week.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when the group shared out his paragraphs?
qa.a: He looked worried at first and then very relieved when the others took his paragraphs and gave him an easier job.

qa.q: What made the halfway check-in useful?
qa.a: It showed the missing paragraphs early, while there was still time to share them out and finish on time.

qa.q: How might Nisha see taking on two extra paragraphs?
qa.a: Nisha agreed to take two, so Nisha probably saw it as fair help for someone who had been ill.

grounding: Shows a group checking in halfway, finding an ill member's writing undone, sharing his paragraphs and giving him an easier job so they finish on time.

subtype: Approach: checking in halfway and reassigning slow tasks [Revision]
passage: Halfway through the week, Tanuja gathered her group under the neem tree behind the school. 'Let's see where we are.' Pinki's drawings were done. Tanuja's map of their block was done. Suraj's writing about the local crops had only two lines. He'd been sick with a cough for four days, and he kept his eyes on the ground. Tanuja thought for a moment. 'Pinki and I will each write one of your parts. You colour the map borders and paste the photos. Okay?' Suraj looked up. 'Okay.' On Saturday the chart was pinned on the classroom wall, a day before the deadline, with Suraj's neat borders around every village.

qa.q: Where did Tanuja gather her group?
qa.a: Under the neem tree behind the school.

qa.q: How did Suraj seem to feel before Tanuja's plan?
qa.a: He kept his eyes on the ground, so he seemed embarrassed and worried about his unfinished part.

qa.q: What else could the group do to catch problems earlier next time?
qa.a: Check in at a set point every week; the halfway check is what let them reshare the work and still finish early.

qa.q: How did the new plan change things for Suraj?
qa.a: Suraj got a job he could manage after being ill, colouring borders, and his neat work ended up on the finished chart.

grounding: Illustrates a group checking progress midway, sharing out an ill member's unwritten part and giving him an easier task, so the project is finished in time.

subtype: Approach: dividing the price by weekly pocket money [Thinking]
passage: The red remote-control car in the shop window cost Rs 600, and Thomas had nothing saved. His elder brother Yogesh laughed. "Six hundred? On your pocket money? Forget it." It was raining, and they were sheltering under the shop's awning, waiting for the bus. Thomas pressed his nose to the glass and did the sum in his head. Fifty rupees every Saturday. Fifty, a hundred, a hundred and fifty... too slow to count. Then he tried dividing. 600 divided by 50. Twelve. Twelve Saturdays. "That's only three months," he said aloud. "Before my birthday, even." Yogesh stopped laughing. Thomas took one last look at the car and got on the bus, already counting.

qa.q: How much does Thomas get each Saturday?
qa.a: Fifty rupees every Saturday.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel once he worked out twelve Saturdays?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and determined, because twelve Saturdays, about three months, seemed reachable.

qa.q: What else could Thomas do to stay on track?
qa.a: Mark the twelve Saturdays on a calendar and share his plan with his parents; dividing the price made the goal feel possible.

qa.q: How does Yogesh see Thomas's plan after the sum?
qa.a: Yogesh stops laughing, so he seems surprised the goal is more reachable than he thought.

grounding: Shows a boy dividing a Rs 600 toy car's price by his Rs 50 weekly pocket money, getting twelve weeks, and deciding it is reachable.

subtype: Approach: dividing the price by weekly pocket money [Thinking]
passage: At his friend's birthday in their Chennai colony, Lalit had driven a remote-control car around the living room for ten whole minutes. Back home, he asked Appa how much one cost. "About Rs 600." Lalit sat at the dining table with a notebook, his sister Simran peering over. "I get Rs 50 every Sunday. So..." He wrote 600 ÷ 50 and worked it out slowly. "Twelve. Twelve Sundays." Simran counted on her fingers. "That's till the end of March." Lalit tapped the pencil. Twelve didn't sound like forever. Twelve was the number of chapters in his science book, and he'd finished those. "Okay," he said. "I'm doing it." He drew twelve boxes on the page.

qa.q: What did Lalit draw on the page?
qa.a: Twelve boxes.

qa.q: Why did twelve not seem like forever to Lalit?
qa.a: He felt confident, comparing it to the twelve science chapters he had already finished, so the goal seemed reachable.

qa.q: What else could Lalit talk over with Appa?
qa.a: Where to keep the money safe each Sunday and whether the price might change; working out twelve weeks gave him a clear goal.

qa.q: How does Simran see Lalit's plan?
qa.a: Simran helps count to the end of March, so she seems interested and supportive.

grounding: Illustrates a boy dividing a Rs 600 toy's price by his Rs 50 a week, finding twelve weeks, and deciding the goal is reachable.

subtype: Approach: putting coins in a jar and marking a chart [Action]
passage: Note on the fridge for Sunaina's parents, from Nani. Our Sunaina is very serious about her savings for the sketching set. She has labelled her clay piggy bank 'SKETCH SET' in big letters and drawn a tall thermometer on chart paper next to her bed. Every Sunday, after her coins go in, she colours one more section red. Today it is up to halfway. Twice this week Rekha asked her to come and buy candy floss at the fair, and twice she looked at the thermometer and said no. I didn't say a word, only told her she is patient. I think we should let her finish it herself.

qa.q: What did Sunaina write on her piggy bank?
qa.a: 'SKETCH SET', in big letters.

qa.q: What does Sunaina looking at the thermometer before saying no suggest?
qa.a: She seemed determined and proud of the red climbing to halfway, and didn't want to undo it.

qa.q: What might help Sunaina stay motivated in the second half?
qa.a: Keeping the thermometer where she sees it every day and talking with her parents about the plan; the rising colour is what keeps her going.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Sunaina saying no twice?
qa.a: Rekha might feel a bit disappointed not to have company at the fair, or puzzled until she hears about the sketching set.

grounding: Shows a girl with a labelled piggy bank and a thermometer chart she colours weekly, whose rising colour keeps her from spending the coins.

subtype: Approach: putting coins in a jar and marking a chart [Action]
passage:
Sunday
Coins in the jar: done! The jar says ROLLER SKATES on masking tape, in my best letters. Then I coloured this week's part of the thermometer on my door. It's up to the line I drew for 'nearly there'. When I started in June, it was just an empty glass shape, and I kept wanting to spend on snacks. Now I like watching the red climb more than I like samosas. Well, almost. Pooja came over and said, 'Noor, just get the cheap ones from the fair.' I showed her the thermometer. She said, 'Okay, fine, it's pretty.' Two more colourings and I'm there.

qa.q: What is written on Noor's jar?
qa.a: ROLLER SKATES, on masking tape.

qa.q: How does Noor feel about watching the red climb?
qa.a: Noor feels proud and motivated, enjoying the rising colour more than snacks, almost 😊

qa.q: What else could Noor do if tempted near the end?
qa.a: Look at the thermometer again, as Noor did with Pooja, or talk the plan over with a parent; the chart keeps the goal visible.

qa.q: How does Pooja come to see the chart?
qa.a: Pooja first suggests cheap skates, then admits the thermometer is pretty, so she seems to warm to the idea.

grounding: Illustrates a girl dropping coins into a labelled jar and colouring a thermometer chart each week, the rising colour keeping her motivated to save.

subtype: Approach: spending on snacks and forgetting the goal [Pitfall]
passage: Mehak, you want to know why I always ask where your pocket money goes? When your Dadu Pradeep was nine, I wanted a real cricket bat, the willow kind. Every Monday my father gave me a few coins, and every Monday I said, 'This goes in the tin.' But the shop near school sold salted chips in paper cones, and cricket stickers in little packets. One cone, one packet, it felt like nothing. After a month I shook the tin. Two coins rattled inside. I sat on the floor and counted every cone I could remember. It was the bat, all of it, gone into my stomach and my sticker book.

qa.q: What did the shop near school sell?
qa.a: Salted chips in paper cones and cricket stickers in little packets.

qa.q: How might young Pradeep have felt when he shook the tin?
qa.a: He probably felt shocked and disappointed, hearing only two coins after a month.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have kept the money for the bat?
qa.a: Putting the coins in the tin before passing the shop, or noting each small spend so he'd see them adding up.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's father have seen the empty tin?
qa.a: His father had given coins every Monday, so he might have felt disappointed, or hoped his son would learn from counting the cones.

grounding: Shows a child spending weekly money on chips and stickers at the shop near school until, after a month, the tin is nearly empty.

subtype: Approach: spending on snacks and forgetting the goal [Pitfall]
passage: All through May the heat was terrible, and the shop right outside the school gate had a freezer of ice lollies and a rack of glitter stickers. Lavanya was saving for a set of watercolours. Every Monday Amma gave her pocket money, and every Monday she promised herself it was going straight into the jar. But at 3 pm, sticky and hot, Parul would say, 'One lolly?' and Lavanya would think, just this once. Stickers on Wednesday. Chips on Friday. She never wrote any of it down. On the last day of the month she tipped the jar out on her bed. Three coins. She stared at them, then at the empty space on her shelf where the paint box was meant to go.

qa.q: What was Lavanya saving for?
qa.a: A set of watercolours.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when she tipped out the jar?
qa.a: She stared at the three coins, so she felt shocked and disappointed that the small spends had eaten her savings.

qa.q: What could Lavanya try next month?
qa.a: Put the money in the jar the moment Amma gives it and note any spend, perhaps with Amma's help, so small treats don't go unnoticed.

qa.q: How might Parul see her 'One lolly?' now?
qa.a: Parul only meant to share a treat in the heat and may not have known Lavanya was saving, so she might feel sorry if she found out.

grounding: Illustrates a child buying lollies, stickers and chips near school each week without counting, and finding the savings jar nearly empty after a month.

subtype: Approach: earning extra by doing jobs at home [Action]
passage: Last year I wanted a Rs 240 kite-making kit, the big one with the spinning reel. My pocket money was Rs 20 a week, so I worked it out: twelve weeks. That felt like forever. So one Saturday I asked Papa and my mother, Sharmila, 'If I wash the car every Sunday, can I get Rs 10?' Papa looked at Ma. Ma said, 'Properly, with the bucket, not just splashing.' Every Sunday morning I washed it: soap, rinse, dry with the old towel, even the wheels. Rs 20 plus Rs 10 made Rs 30 a week. I did the maths again. Eight weeks! I got the kit four weeks sooner, and Papa said, 'Tarun beta, this car has never been so clean.'

qa.q: How much did Tarun earn for each car wash?
qa.a: Rs 10 every Sunday.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel about waiting twelve weeks?
qa.a: Twelve weeks felt like forever, so Tarun was impatient and keen to find a quicker way.

qa.q: Why was asking his parents first a good step?
qa.a: They agreed on the job and how it should be done, like washing properly with the bucket, so the extra money was fair and clear.

qa.q: How did Papa see the Sunday washes?
qa.a: Papa said the car had never been so clean, so he seemed pleased with the arrangement.

grounding: Shows a boy asking his parents to earn Rs 10 for washing the car on Sundays, cutting his saving time from twelve weeks to eight.

subtype: Approach: earning extra by doing jobs at home [Action]
passage: Note in the family diary, Sunday. Last week Tejas asked if he could earn Rs 10 by washing the car every Sunday. He's saving for a Rs 240 cricket set like his friend Irfan's, and on his Rs 20 a week it would take twelve weeks. We agreed, on condition that he does it properly. This morning he was up at seven with the bucket, the old towel and the brush for the tyres. It took him forty minutes. He came in soaked, held out his hand for the Rs 10, and then wrote in his little notebook: 'Rs 30 a week now. 8 weeks!' I've put a star on the calendar eight Sundays from today.

qa.q: How long did the car wash take Tejas?
qa.a: It took him forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Tejas seem to feel when he wrote '8 weeks!'?
qa.a: He seemed excited and proud that his own work had cut the wait from twelve weeks to eight.

qa.q: What made this plan work?
qa.a: Tejas asked first and agreed a clear job with his family, then kept to it, which shortened his wait.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Tejas's effort?
qa.a: The note-writer notices him up at seven doing it properly and backs the goal by starring the calendar.

grounding: Illustrates a boy agreeing with his family to earn Rs 10 by washing the car each Sunday, shortening his wait from twelve weeks to eight.

subtype: Approach: comparing shops and cheaper choices [Thinking]
passage:
"Ira Apa, look. The block set at the big toy shop is Rs 900."
"Too much."
"But the stationery shop near the mosque has the same box. Same picture, same number of pieces. Rs 800."
"So a hundred less. Good find."
"And there's a smaller set, just the house, for Rs 500."
"So get that one sooner?"
Sabina frowned at her savings notebook. "The big one has the garden and the car. I'd play with those a lot. The small one I'd finish building in one day."
"So?"
"So... I've got Rs 350 now. The small one is about a month away. The big one from the stationery shop is two months more. But I'd use it longer." She chewed her pen. "I think the big one. From the cheaper shop."

qa.q: How much is the same block set at the stationery shop?
What was Sabina feeling as she chewed her pen?
qa.a: She felt torn between getting the small set sooner and waiting longer for the big one she'd play with more.

qa.q: What else could Sabina check before deciding?
qa.a: Ask a parent to help confirm the cheaper shop's box is really the same and complete; comparing shops and sizes helped her choose.

qa.q: How does Ira seem to see Sabina's thinking?
qa.a: Ira calls it a good find and asks simple questions, letting Sabina work it out, so Ira seems supportive.

grounding: Shows a girl finding the same toy Rs 100 cheaper elsewhere and a smaller set for less, then weighing whether the extra pieces are worth a longer wait.

subtype: Approach: comparing shops and cheaper choices [Thinking]
passage: Last winter I was saving for a doll's house kit, and I thought I knew the price: Rs 1,200 at the big toy shop. Then my brother Naveen came back from the market and said, 'Sudha didi, the shop behind the bus stand has it for Rs 1,100.' Same box; I went and checked myself. Then I found a smaller kit, just two rooms, for Rs 700. I had Rs 600 and saved Rs 50 a week. I could get the small one in two weeks! I sat on my bed with both boxes in my head. The big one had a staircase and a garden, and I knew I'd keep adding to it for years. The small one I'd get bored of. So I waited ten weeks and bought the big one from the bus stand shop.

qa.q: What price did Naveen find behind the bus stand?
How did Sudha feel when she saw she could get the small kit in two weeks?
qa.a: Sudha felt excited and tempted, because it was so much sooner.

qa.q: What helped Sudha choose, and what else could she have checked?
qa.a: Picturing how long she'd enjoy each kit; she could also have asked a parent whether the cheaper shop's box was complete.

qa.q: How might Naveen see his market discovery?
qa.a: Naveen found the cheaper shop for her, so he may feel pleased and helpful when she buys from there.

grounding: Illustrates a girl comparing shops, finding the same kit Rs 100 cheaper and a smaller one for less, and weighing whether the extras are worth waiting for.
